Run smarter agents. Use fewer tokens. Our code review bill went up 36x this year. Now a review costs us 18 cents. See how ↓ Quickstart · Case studies · Tour · Templates · Deploy · Docs AgentRun is an open-source platform that supercharges your agents. It adds self-improvement, durable execution and a control plane on top of your favorite agent harness. Your agents become smarter, more fault tolerant and use fewer tokens with every run. An agent's Learning tab: what it kept, and what changed since. Demo data from the console's recorded fixtures. Code review. Greptile started charging a dollar a review in March, then our agents took off, and our bill went from $180 a month to $6,451. So we built our own reviewer on a cheap model and tuned it on our own PRs. It costs 18 cents a review, and on 30 PRs it had never seen it caught 1.6x the real bugs Greptile did. How we built it · Tune one on your repo Merchant codes. We let Opus figure out how to classify merchants, then handed what it learned to a cheap model. Same job, $0.89 down to $0.12 a merchant. How it works · Do it with your own job Agents are great at figuring things out. The problem is they figure out the same things over and over. Give an agent a job it has done a hundred times and it rediscovers the same API, rereads the same docs and rebuilds the same plan, and you pay for every token of it. Bring your agent on the harness it runs best on: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or pi. AgentRun does everything around it: You don't build the plumbing: provider integrations, recovery, run tracking and learning are all here. Run it on your laptop with one command, in one container, or as a server with runners. Apache-2.0. You need Node 24.22.3 or newer, on macOS or Linux. Start it. npx @parcha/agentrun It starts the server and one runner on port 7340 (or the next free one), keeps everything in ~/.agentrun , and opens the console in your browser. Add one model key. In the console, set a password, then add a key under Settings → Model keys . One OPENROUTER_API_KEY gives every harness a model. An Anthropic key runs pi and Claude Code; an OpenAI key runs pi, Codex and OpenCode. Run your first agent. Open Templates , apply KYB due diligence , and start a run with a company's name and website. It needs nothing but your model key. When it finishes, the run's Report tab has a due diligence report with a verdict and every claim cited. Then open the agent's Learning tab to see what it kept for next time. Rather have your coding agent do it? Tell it: Read agentrun.ai/SKILL.md and set up AgentRun for me . If Docker is running on your machine, new agents get a Docker sandbox with a shell. Its image builds on first use, which takes a few minutes, and the console says when it's ready. Without Docker, agents still read and write files, but get no shell. Want your own server with a URL? Deploy it to Render in one click. Workflows that make the call. A step can ask a fast typed question, see how sure the answer is, and pick a route. Here the model leans approve at 0.61, below the workflow's 0.75 bar, so the case goes to review. Every agent in one place. Mission Control opens first: what needs you, what failed, what's running and what it cost, by day, by harness and by tool. Every agent is an API. Start a run from the Playground, then copy the same request into your code. You stay in control. An agent can stop and ask you, and the run waits until you answer. Turn it on with "learning": true in an agent's definition. At the end of every run, the agent gets one more turn to say what it would keep. AgentRun checks it, grades it, and commits the keepers to the agent's own git folder. The next run starts from there. flowchart LR start["Run starts from
the agent's main"] --> work["Run does the job"] work --> propose["Last turn proposes
notes, a skill, a workflow"] propose --> check["Code checks,
then one grader"] check -->|kept| commit["Commit to main"] commit --> start Loading Notes are short markdown files, one fact each, in Claude Code's memory format. Skills are how to do a job again, and only a run that finished the job can write one. Learned workflows run as one tool call on any harness, under the run's own cap and tool permissions. Once a learned skill has served 3 runs, the next run is asked for that job as a workflow draft, and a draft is dry-run before it's kept: no model is asked and no tool runs. The agent's Learning tab shows every note, skill and workflow and the log of changes, and each run shows which notes it was given and opened. Retire anything there, or with npx @parcha/agentrun learning retire and the note's ETag. Git keeps the history, so a retired note can come back. Each agent has a learning folder: plain git with one branch, main . A run reads the index of active notes in its instructions and gets the learned skills beside its own. Code checks every proposal first. An item that breaks a rule of its own (a size or count limit, its name, its shape) is left out and the rest goes on. A secret or a hidden character anywhere in the answer, a file outside the folder, a deletion or a full index drops the whole answer, since no item of it can be trusted. Then one grader judges what it says, and AgentRun commits what passes. A risky rule waits for your OK. A rule the run found in a page or a pasted email, or a note that holds an account number, is dropped. Once an agent's notes outgrow the learning budget, each run gets the ones that bear on its first message, whole, and a line for each of the rest. A run that only ran a learned workflow isn't asked what to keep. A lot of agents don't need to be agents. Write repeatable work as a typed workflow: tool calls, model steps and fast typed decisions (yes or no, pick one, a score, each with its confidence), with an agent to fall back on when a case is unclear. AgentRun runs it as an agent's revision, under the agent's tool permissions and a cap like any run, and a trigger can start one. An illustration of the control flow in examples/support-answer.mjs , not a recording of a model run. Watch any workflow run node by node, pause it and resume it, and read every decision and why it was made: A workflow is a JSON document of typed steps: { "v" : 2 , "name" : " read-site " , "schemas" : { "In" : { "type" : " object " , "required" : [ " website " ], "properties" : { "website" : { "type" : " string " } } }, "Page" : { "type" : " object " , "required" : [ " ok " ], "properties" : { "ok" : { "type" : " boolean " } } } }, "input" : { "schemaId" : " In " }, "output" : { "schemaId" : " Page " , "path" : " home " }, "root" : { "node" : " chain " , "steps" : [ { "node" : " call " , "label" : " Read the home page " , "via" : " tool " , "tool" : " web_fetch " , "args" : { "url" : " {website} " }, "out" : " Page " , "as" : " home " , "deadline_s" : 60 } ] } } Steps can call tools, run a model, ask a fast typed question, branch on the answer, map over a list in parallel, loop a bounded number of times, call other workflows, or hand the hard case to an agent. Save one as an agent's workflow field; npx @parcha/agentrun workflows validate checks it first. The workflow language also runs on its own inside your app, with a TypeScript builder . Every agent, revision, run and step lives in one store. Stop the server mid-run and start it again, and the run carries on. With several runners, another runner picks up a dead runner's runs once their 30-second lease runs out. A finished step is never run again; a write a crash cut off mid-call is marked interrupted rather than retried, so you can check it. Five ready-made agents. Apply one in one screen, make it yours, and measure it with its own eval cases. Each template is one folder: the agent's instructions, its skills, its rules and its eval cases. Templates → Apply grants nothing until you tick each MCP tool yourself. npx @parcha/agentrun template eval DIR runs a template's eval cases as real runs on a throwaway server and grades them. Template packages has the folder format. Want a template to know your code? Tune a template on your own code walks through the loop we ran on code-review . Triggers start capped runs on their own: schedules, signed webhooks and GitHub pull request events. Harnesses. Name one in the agent's definition with harness . Approvals, caps, computers, triggers and learning work the same on each. npx @parcha/agentrun server capabilities says which harnesses your server runs. Computers. An agent gets a computer with one setting. It gets the tools for that kind and nothing else, and changing the computer changes nothing else about the agent. computer : kind : sandbox # none, sandbox, desktop, phone or browser provider : daytona # one you connected in Settings → Computers (none takes no provider) Kind What the agent can do Providers none Read and write files in its run folder; no shell (with Archil, commands run on Archil's exec) none needed sandbox Run code, install packages, keep processes in the background, on Linux Docker, Daytona, Modal, E2B desktop See a Linux screen, move the mouse, type Orgo, E2B, Docker (your own image with an X server) phone Tap, swipe, type, open apps and read the screen on Android phone harness (a rented cloud Android) browser Browse the web, and hand the controls to you at any point Browserbase, Kernel Every kind but none names its provider. An agent with no computer setting gets the Docker sandbox where the server has Docker, and no computer otherwise. Remote computers bill through your own account with the vendor. @parcha/agentrun-computer is the protocol underneath: one small daemon in every computer and one provider per vendor. flowchart LR you["Console · CLI · API"] --> server["Server"] server --> store["One store
SQLite or Postgres"] runner["Runners"] -->|claim runs| store runner --> hands["Hands
run folder + computer"] Loading Server. Serves the API at /v2 and the console. It writes runs and commands to the store and reads it back for you. It runs no agent loop itself when you start it with --no-runner . Store. Agents, revisions, runs and every run's journal, in one place. SQLite in the data folder by default, or Postgres with AGENTRUN_STORE_URL . Runners. Each runner claims runs from the store and runs many at once. Every approval check, cap and model call happens here. Add runners to scale out. Hands. Where the agent's tools act. Each run has a run folder for its files. A sandbox mounts that folder at /workspace and the tools run inside it; a desktop, phone or browser leaves the folder on the runner. From the terminal and from code npx @parcha/agentrun is also the server's CLI. Run these in a second terminal while the server is up; the CLI finds it and its token by itself. The script makes an agent, starts a run capped at $1, lets the agent ask you a question, answers it, and reads the file the agent wrote. With Docker on, the first run waits for the sandbox image. # 1. Make an agent that can write files and ask you things. cat > agent.json << ' EOF ' {"definition": {"id": "notes", "version": 1, "name": "Notes", "instructions": "Do what you are asked, and write what you make to a file.", "skills": [], "tools": ["write", "ask_person"]}} EOF npx @parcha/agentrun agents create --body @agent.json # 2. Start a capped run and wait. It stops to ask you which region (exit code 8: it waits on you). npx @parcha/agentrun runs start notes --max-cost-usd 1 --wait \ --body ' {"input": {"content": "Ask me which region to cover, then write region.md about it."}} ' > out.json # 3. Answer, wait for it to finish, and read what it wrote. run= $( node -p ' require("./out.json").run_id ' ) npx @parcha/agentrun runs message " $run " --content " Europe " npx @parcha/agentrun runs wait " $run " > out.json npx @parcha/agentrun runs read-file " $run " region.md runs wait exits 0 when the run completed, 1 when it failed, and 8 when it waits on you: a question, its cap, or an approval. runs timeline RUN_ID --follow streams each step as it happens, and every run carries a console_url to its page. npx @parcha/agentrun help lists every command; npx @parcha/agentrun skill install --claude (or --codex ) teaches your coding agent the CLI. With the TypeScript client ( npm install @parcha/agentrun-client , no dependencies). The client reads its server and token from the environment; the server prints both when it starts (with npx @parcha/agentrun , the token is in ~/.agentrun/.token , and the address is normally http://127.0.0.1:7340 ): export AGENTRUN_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:7340/v2 export AGENTRUN_API_KEY= $( cat ~ /.agentrun/.token ) import { AgentRun } from "@parcha/agentrun-client" ; const client = new AgentRun ( ) ; // AGENTRUN_BASE_URL and AGENTRUN_API_KEY const started = await client . runs . start ( "notes" , { input : { content : "Ask me which region to cover, then write region.md about it." } , max_cost_usd : 1 } ) ; let run = await client . runs . wait ( started . run_id ) ; if ( run . pending ?. kind === "question" ) await client . runs . message ( run . run_id , { content : "Europe" } ) ; run = await client . runs . wait ( run . run_id ) ; console . log ( run . status , run . cost . usd ) ; The Python client is pip install parcha-agentrun , with the same methods ( TypeScript client , Python client ). Render, in one click. The button deploys render.yaml : one 1 CPU / 2 GB instance with a 10 GB disk, the published image (no build), and the token and seal key generated for you. It needs a card on your Render workspace: about $25 a month for the instance and $2.50 for the disk, at Render's prices when this was written. In Render's form, paste OPENROUTER_API_KEY . We recommend an OpenRouter key with a dollar cap and an expiration date. Do not share this key with anyone. When it's live, open its URL and paste AGENTRUN_TOKEN from the service's Environment tab to set your password. On a Linux machine with Docker: git clone https://github.com/Parcha-ai/agentrun && cd agentrun/deploy printf ' AGENTRUN_SEAL_KEY=%s\n ' " $( openssl rand -base64 32 ) " > .env && chmod 600 .env echo ' OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... ' >> .env docker compose up -d --build docker compose logs server # the console's link, the first visit's setup code and, the first time, the token The port is published on this machine's loopback only; put a TLS proxy in front before you open it to anyone else. This compose file has no Docker socket, so its agents get file tools and web_fetch but no shell. For a Docker sandbox, use the single-server compose.yaml at the repository's root (Docker Engine 26 or later), run the server on the host, or use a Daytona or E2B computer with an Archil disk. Set AGENTRUN_STORE_URL to a postgres:// URL on the server and every runner (the compose file's pg profile runs one), start the server with --no-runner , and start each runner from the same image with runner --data /data --name . Give every process the same AGENTRUN_SEAL_KEY . Runners still share the /data volume in this release. Deploying AgentRun covers runners, health checks and upgrades. Every saved secret (model and tool keys, MCP credentials, sign-ins, webhook signing secrets) is sealed under one key, AGENTRUN_SEAL_KEY ; keep it, because losing it loses what it sealed. Secrets are write-only: the console shows each one as set or missing, and only the console can paste, replace or remove one (your signed-in session, or the launcher's console on loopback when accounts are off). A key set where the server starts wins over a pasted one. The API token can't write a secret or approve a tool call. A run gets only the keys its own model and tools need, and nothing a run learns can keep a secret it was handed. SECURITY.md says how to report a vulnerability. Apache-2.0.
